### 3. Threads (< 500 chars)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Just built a visual explainer for SO(3) — the math behind every 3D rotation in games, robotics, and physics.

The wild part? 3D rotations don't commute. Try it: rotate something 90° around X then Y. Now do Y then X. Different result!

That's why we need Lie groups. The exponential map exp: so(3) → SO(3) connects infinitesimal rotations to actual rotation matrices via Rodrigues' formula.

Also implemented quaternions — they avoid gimbal lock and compose efficiently.

### 4. Mastodon (< 500 chars)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Deep dive into SO(3), the Special Orthogonal Group in 3 dimensions.

Implemented in Python:
• Hat map: R³ → so(3) (skew-symmetric matrices)
• Rodrigues' formula: exp([ω]×) = I + (sin θ/θ)[ω]× + ((1-cos θ)/θ²)[ω]×²
• Quaternion representation: q = (cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)·n)
• Geodesic interpolation on SO(3)

Verified the Lie bracket commutation relations: [Lx, Ly] = Lz (cyclic)

The BCH formula error plot shows why exp(X)exp(Y) ≠ exp(X+Y) for non-commuting rotations.

### 5. Reddit (Title + Body for r/learnpython or r/math)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**Title:** I built a visual explainer for SO(3) — the Lie group of 3D rotations — in Python

**Body:**

Ever wondered why 3D rotations are so tricky? Why does your robot arm sometimes twist unexpectedly, or why do game engines use quaternions?

The answer lies in SO(3), the "Special Orthogonal group in 3 dimensions." It's a Lie group — meaning it's both a smooth surface (manifold) and a group (you can compose rotations).

**What I implemented:**

1. **The Hat Map** — Converts a 3D vector ω to a skew-symmetric matrix [ω]×. This matrix encodes infinitesimal rotations.

2. **Rodrigues' Formula** — The exponential map from the Lie algebra to the Lie group:
   R = I + (sin θ / θ)[ω]× + ((1 - cos θ) / θ²)[ω]×²

   This converts axis-angle representation directly to a rotation matrix.

3. **Non-commutativity demonstration** — Rotating 90° about X then Y gives a DIFFERENT result than Y then X. The visualization makes this crystal clear.

4. **Quaternion conversion** — Unit quaternions q = (cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)·n) parameterize SO(3) without gimbal lock.

5. **Geodesic interpolation** — Smoothly interpolate between two rotations using log and exp maps.

**ELI5 version:** Imagine you're holding a book. Tilt it forward, then rotate it right. Now start over: rotate right first, then tilt forward. The book ends up in different orientations! That's non-commutativity, and SO(3) is the mathematical framework that explains it.

The Jupyter notebook has all the code and visualizations. You can run it yourself and play with the parameters.

**View the interactive notebook:** https://cocalc.com/github/Ok-landscape/computational-pipeline/blob/main/notebooks/published/lie_groups_so3_rotation.ipynb

### 6. Facebook (< 500 chars)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Did you know that 3D rotations don't work the way you'd expect?

Try this: Take a book. Rotate it 90° forward, then 90° to the right. Now reset and do it the other way — right first, then forward. Different result!

This is SO(3), the mathematics behind every 3D video game, robot, and satellite. I built a Python notebook exploring how it works, including the famous Rodrigues' formula and quaternions.

Check it out: https://cocalc.com/github/Ok-landscape/computational-pipeline/blob/main/notebooks/published/lie_groups_so3_rotation.ipynb

Exploring the Mathematics Behind Robotics and 3D Graphics: SO(3) and Lie Groups

I recently built an educational Jupyter notebook diving into SO(3) — the Special Orthogonal Group that governs all rotations in three-dimensional space.

Key implementations:
• Rodrigues' rotation formula converting axis-angle to rotation matrices
• The hat/vee maps between R³ and the Lie algebra so(3)
• Quaternion representation for singularity-free rotation composition
• Geodesic interpolation on the SO(3) manifold
• Visualization of non-commutativity and the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula

Why this matters: Understanding SO(3) is essential for anyone working in robotics (inverse kinematics, motion planning), computer graphics (camera systems, animation), aerospace (attitude control), or physics simulations.

The notebook includes verified implementations, mathematical derivations, and visualizations showing why rotation order matters — a concept that trips up many engineers.

### 8. Instagram (< 500 chars, visual-focused caption)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The hidden math behind every 3D rotation

This plot shows something surprising: 3D rotations don't commute.

Rotate X then Y → blue arrow
Rotate Y then X → red arrow

Same rotations, different order, different result.

That's SO(3), the Lie group that powers robotics, games, and spacecraft navigation.

The bottom-right graph shows the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff correction — proving exp(X)exp(Y) ≠ exp(X+Y) when things don't commute.

Math is beautiful when you can see it.
